extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of satirical/ comic Renaissance prose; students of humor and literary satire
extracted.subtask_description: Producing or analysing comic, satirical prose in the broad Rabelaisian mode: grotesque exaggeration, institutional parody, earthy bodily humour, neologisms, and mock-scholarly asides. Useful for authors imitating Renaissance satirical novels or critics describing their techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody institutions to expose corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Create fictional bureaucratic/legal institutions and officers that mirror real-world corruption and venality (e.g., 'Gripe-men-all', 'Furred Law-cats').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use grotesque, evocative names and scenes of ritual to show systemic greed and incompetence (example lines: 'The Furred Law-cats no sooner heard the jingling of the chink...'; courts that demand payment: 'The court... finds the prisoners not guilty, and accordingly orders them to be discharged out of custody, paying their fees.'). The parody can dramatize bribery, extractive assessments, and procedural absurdity to generate satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque bodily and coarse humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ crude, bodily, and scatological images for comic shock and earthy realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make fearless use of coarse expressions and bodily functions as punchlines or comic emphasis (examples: 'what comes out at my bunghole were beans', repeated curses and expletives). These register-low elements contrast with high rhetoric to produce humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive names and neologisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Coin compounds, literal-sounding epithets, and mock-legal/archaic words to create comedic effect (e.g., 'Refusing-of-fees', 'Twofold', 'Double-fee').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neologisms can encode satire directly (a name signals a vice or institutional role). Vary formation (hyphenation, translation-like calques, mock-Latin) for texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended metaphor and allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustain large metaphors or allegories (e.g., a wine-press as the legal/administrative machine) to critique social practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map parts of the allegorical object to institutional terms (the text maps press parts to legal/financial vocabulary: 'spindle... receipt; the trough, cost and damages; the hole for the vice-pin, state'). The long, coherent metaphor deepens satire by showing systemic extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogues and accumulative lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use long, detailed lists of objects or ingredients to build comic excess and illustrate greed or abundance (e.g., cargo lists, food lists, items squeezed from the press).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put many concrete items in succession ('venison, hares, capons, turkeys, pigs, swine, bacon, kids, calves, hens, ducks, teals, geese...') to create rhythm, overwhelm the reader, and make a point about consumption or corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix high/classical references with low material
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtapose learned, mythological, or classical allusions (Hercules, Pythagoras, Ulysses) with base events or coarse behaviour to comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke mythic exemplars and then undercut them with vulgar comparisons or literal-minded parody (e.g., 'What made Hercules such a famous fellow... he destroyed robbers... Why then do we not follow his example' followed by coarse talk). This contrast lampoons pretensions to nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riddle and anticlimax as comic device
rubrics_metrics.description: Include enigmatic riddles or pseudo-philosophical puzzles that receive absurd or earthy solutions (the enigma about the mite/weevil born of a bean).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the set-up promise high meaning or erudition, then resolve in a grotesque naturalistic answer, exposing pretension and producing laughter through reversal and disproportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue rhythm, refrains and interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use repeated refrains ('Give, give me out of hand—an answer.') and characters breaking into one another's speech to produce comic timing and escalating absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short repeated phrases, interruptions, whispered asides, and parenthetical retorts sustain tempo and build verbal comedy; stage the ensemble so each character's mannerism becomes a running gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register contrast (learned vs coarse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate between mock-scholarly language, Latinisms, and the coarsest curses to create comic tension and reveal hypocrisy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sprinkle decretals, legalistic phraseology, or learned-sounding glosses amid curses, slang, or fart jokes (examples: 'By the memory of the decretals...' next to 'Ods-belly' or 'a shitten one'). The clash highlights pretence and satirizes institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character caricature and stock-types
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct exaggerated, recognizable comic types (the greedy lawyer, vainglorious friar, crafty protagonist) whose defining trait is repeatedly shown in speech and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give characters a dominant comic trait and scenes that let that trait play out in multiple ways (Friar John's violent generosity, Panurge's cowardly wit). Repetition cements the caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parodic etymology and glossing
rubrics_metrics.description: Create mock etymologies, glosses, or labels that reinterpret ordinary institutions or objects in satirical ways ('applied part names mapped to legal vocabulary').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer faux-linguistic explanations and label-mappings to expose the absurdity of official terminology (the wine-press parts named 'receipt', 'cost and damages', 'authentic decrees'). This technique satirizes bureaucratic language by literalizing its function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical slapstick and action-based gags
rubrics_metrics.description: Stage physical comedy within the prose—theatrical gestures, thefts amid feathers, threats brandished but leading to flight—to create visual humour in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe rapid, physical episodes (Friar John ripping a bed's feathers and taking the blanket) with energetic verbs to produce a slapstick sequence that complements verbal wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony through reversal and moral indictment
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ironic reversal (courts that exist to punish the poor but protect the great; 'laws are like cobwebs' that catch the weak) to indict institutions and create dark comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present ostensible virtues that operate inversely in practice. Let statements read as official (the court's pronouncements) reveal the opposite when enacted; the tension between declarative language and outcome fuels satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock-editorial/footnote as meta-humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert editorial parentheticals or translator's notes that comment ironically on the narrative (e.g., Motteux's explanatory note about Calpe/Abyla).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bracketed notes or translator's asides to add another layer of comedy—self-conscious commentary, pseudo-erudition, or reader-address that undercuts the text or amplifies its joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory detail and setting as comic tableau
rubrics_metrics.description: Render settings with vivid sensory detail (the crowded press, the jingling purse, the darkened feathers) to ground the satire and provide material for jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete textures, sounds, and smells make absurd scenes believable and heighten humour when contrasted with the actions or rhetoric of agents in the scene.
